en: Truth, knowledge, infinite, one, stainless, destroyer of darkness, supreme, non-dual, residing in the center of the heart-lotus, the witness of all cognitions,
the object of the wisdom established through the Vedāntas, and perceived as the inner self by yogis— [I bow to that].
Having prostrated before him with devotion, I shall set forth the excellent commentary on the *Vedaśiras*.
Having bowed with devotion to him— who pervades this world with rays of fame resembling the beams of the entire stainless moon, who, overcome by compassion, brought benefit to those in suffering,
and before whose thunderbolt-like speech the intellects of logicians fell shattered in all directions— I now strive in the method of his commentary.
By the grace of my teacher, this commentary on the essence of the Taittirīyaka is being composed by me for those who desire a clear exposition of its meaning. (3)
The obligatory rites prescribed for a Brahmin went toward the destruction of evil,
while the optional rites performed here bear fruits both seen and unseen.

Now, knowledge is introduced as follows, for it brings about the understanding of things as they truly are, and is alone capable of uprooting those causes which lead to the appropriation of karma. (5)

The Śruti has proclaimed that bondage and liberation have as their sole causes, respectively, desire and the absence of desire, saying: "He is according to his desire," and likewise, "He who is without desire. (6)

In reality, which is free from duality and is at all times the very nature of the Self, there is misconception due to lack of realization; from that [misconception] comes desire, and from that, ritual actions.
Since that activity which arises from ignorance would cease upon the knowledge of reality,
therefore, true knowledge is sufficient for the pacification of all activities.

One who seeks liberation should not engage in actions performed for the sake of desire or those that are prohibited; however, one should perform the obligatory and occasional rites with the desire to avoid transgression.
He raises the objection stated in the Bhāṣya beginning with "pratiṣiddhayoḥ" (of the two prohibited [actions]) by saying "mokṣārthī" (one seeking liberation). || 9 ||
Thus, having rejected the claim made by the Mīmāṃsakas and others that ritual action is the means to liberation,
the definitive conclusion regarding this matter is established through reasoning based on the knowledge of the Self.
He refutes [the argument] that "it arises" with the words: "In that case... (10).

This cannot be so, for it would be illogical that [the soul] should receive contradictory results, since according to the teachings of the scriptures, many karmas capable of yielding such results are possible for a person. (11)
There exist here millions of karmas whose fruits have not yet begun;
let the state of those karmas be understood from the expression "those which are here. (12)
Furthermore, the fruits of killing a Brahmin and performing a horse sacrifice do not manifest within a single body,
because they are causes of contradictory results for a foolish person and a person of sattvic nature respectively.
It is heard in the treatises on Dharma that even the effect of a single action here may persist for seven births; how much more so, then, for many actions?

If it is held that [knowledge] is for the destruction of those obligatory rites whose effects have not yet begun, it is not so; for that [knowledge] destroys the very evil which is the cause of activity directed toward one's own self. (15)
The term "transgression" (pratyavāya) refers to the consequence of an evil deed;
its cessation occurs through the obligatory rites (*nitya*) because of their opposition [to such deeds], but not [the cessation] of those [evil deeds] that yield desired fruits.
And desire is the cause of action; its cessation is not possible without the realization of the inner self (pratyagbodha), for it is said that this [cessation] cannot occur otherwise. || 17 ||
Since the self is not the fruit [of action], all ritual activity is prescribed for its sake;
because the self is already attained, there can be no action for the purpose of attaining it. (18)
And since there is no performance of obligatory rites, how could there be a transgression arising from that?
For existence cannot arise from non-existence, because there is no authoritative means of knowledge [for such a claim]. (19)
Therefore, the hundred [strokes] serve as the defining characteristic for that act of transgression which leads one back to the state of being an agent due to previously accumulated karmas.

Since the non-performance of obligatory rites is characterized by the immediate occurrence of a transgression, the suffix *śatṛ* must be used in the sense of a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). (21)
If an entity were to arise from non-existence, there would be a contradiction with all means of valid cognition;
therefore, the claim that the self exists effortlessly is utterly trivial.
He concludes that this is its liberation with the words: "Therefore," || 22 ||
Since you maintain that an extraordinary pleasure which has been shaken off is the cause of karma, it is therefore improper; this is now explained as follows. (23)
Since liberation consists in the state of immutability, action cannot be its means;
for if it were the fruit of action, it would be non-eternal, like heaven and such.
If it is argued that action devoid of knowledge yields impermanent results, whereas for me, action possessed of knowledge yields eternal results; 25.
For one who begins [an action] in this manner, there is a constant connection with impermanence;
nor is knowledge capable of warding off the impermanence that has already been attained. (26)
If liberation were like a non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), then the effect of karma would certainly persist;
since liberation is of the nature of a positive entity (*bhāvātmaka*), it cannot possibly reside within me. (27)
An effect is distinct from its destruction; it is impermanent because it arises through action, like a jar and so forth. Since this qualification is present in the proposition, there is no fault.
From destruction, fragments and the like would arise, and that [destruction] would be impermanent like a jar or other objects;
since it is merely a mental construction, it cannot be produced by actions. (29)
Through appearances and disappearances, all properties such as jars and the like always exist within their substratum, the clay; they do not reside in non-existence. (30)
There is no connection for non-existence with either action or quality;
because it is devoid of self-nature, it is not at all capable of being connected with anything anywhere. (31)
"It does not exist. He clarifies this very point: "Because it is devoid of self-nature" (nirātmakatvāt). || 31 ||

Therefore, for the sake of establishing conventional usage, this non-existence—such as destruction and so forth—should be considered a mere conceptual construction, false like [the metaphorical application of] "son of a stone" and the like. (32)
The meaning is that non-existence imagined by the intellect does not exist as a reality. || 32 ||
Therefore, upon the cessation of ignorance, there would be abiding in the Self;
and the abandonment of ignorance cannot occur anywhere except through the knowledge of Brahman.
Therefore, one should know that the supreme Upaniṣad has been commenced for the sake of knowledge;
it is for the purpose of removing ignorance through service, and it leads knowledge to abide within the Self. 34.
He qualifies that very knowledge with the words: "That same [knowledge]. || 34 ||
Because it completely eradicates the fetters of conception, birth, and so forth for those who practice the knowledge, it is therefore called the *upaniṣad*. (35)
Or, having approached [the teacher], it is that which is seated [in the heart] which is the ultimate good;
therefore, it should be known as the *upaniṣad*, while the book is so called by virtue of its meaning. (36)
Likewise, Mitra is the deity presiding over the vital breath and the day; here, Brahman is entreated: "May there be well-being and happiness for us. (37)
Brahman, which is of such a nature, is sought by one desiring liberation; it is grasped in the sentence by means of the locative case. || 37 ||
May Varuṇa, who presides over the night and the downward movement of breath (apāna), be auspicious to us everywhere; and may the Sun, Aryaman, who resides in the eye, be auspicious to us.
Regarding the sun, he says: "He is the Āditya, and he resides in the eye. (38)

May the Blessed Lord Indra be in our strength, Bṛhaspati in our speech and intellect, and Viṣṇu of the wide stride be in our thighs; for he indeed is the one whose stride is vast. May he grant us peace.
And [the word] "Viṣṇu. He clarifies his quality of wide-striding with the words: "vast" (vistīrṇa). || 39 ||
For in those states of happiness, there would certainly be a lack of pacification. || 40 ||
In this way, hearing, retention, and application are accomplished;
therefore, one should strive for the absence of obstacles to knowledge. (41)
For the sake of pacifying obstacles to the knowledge of Brahman, one who desires to know Brahman should perform the acts of salutation and verbal praise to the one whose form is Vāyu. 42.
Since all fruits of action are indeed dependent upon Brahman, may there always be power for that Vāyu, who is Brahman. (43)
Having paid homage by way of the indirect, there is now homage by way of the direct;
Vāyu alone is designated through both his indirect and manifest forms. (44)
"O Vāyu, you alone are Brahman manifest"—this is the praise.
Therefore, I shall speak of you alone, for you are perceived directly. (45)

"In accordance with the scriptures and according to what must be done, having firmly resolved it in my mind—that which is truth (ṛta), because it depends upon reality (tattva)—I shall speak. This is the connection [of the verse]. (46)
The meaning is that, because of this, the statement "I shall speak of you alone" is indeed a praise of the deity. || 46 ||
That very [truth] residing in practice is designated as "truth";
yet, because that too is dependent upon you, I shall indeed speak of it now. (47)
May the True One, praised by the seeker of knowledge, protect me and my teacher;
may He always protect us both with the power of receiving and imparting knowledge. 48.
The threefold pacification of obstacles to the attainment of knowledge is now described;
for it is through this that both teacher and disciple are able to know Brahman. (49)
Since the Vedāntas are primarily concerned with the knowledge of the meaning for the wise, the instruction (Śikṣā) is set forth so that no effortlessness in recitation may occur. (50)
The meaning is that this [activity] proceeds with this very purpose in mind. || 50 ||
We shall now explain that which is called "training in action. (51)

The letters beginning with 'a' are the phonemes (varṇa), and likewise the acute accent and others are the tones (svara). Short, long, and protracted [vowels] are the measures (mātrā), and effort (prayatna) is known as strength (bala). (52)
"Evenness is the uniformity of vowels and the avoidance of irregularity; continuity, however, is the *saṃhitā*—thus is the training (*śikṣā*) taught. (53)
For those whose minds are inclined toward external objects in order to enter into subtle matters, meditation on the gross is first described as having the *saṃhitā* as its object. (54)
May that fame which arises from causes such as the *saṃhitā* be shared by us both;
likewise, may the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*) belong to both of us, the teacher and the disciple. (55)
This is stated by two sentences; he explains it as follows: "The *saṃhitā* and so forth. (55)
Fame, renown, and illumination arising from the cause of virtuous conduct and Vedic study—this they call *brahmavarcasa*, which is the splendor that has its basis therein. (56)
The meaning is that they employ the term "splendor" (varcasa). || 56 ||
This blessing is to be understood as belonging to the disciple, not to the teacher who has already accomplished his purpose;
for a blessing is indeed appropriate for those who have not yet attained the goals of human endeavor. (57)
Since this knowledge of the *saṃhitā* follows immediately after the mastery of Vedic study and is more proximate [to it], it is therefore described here. (58)
Now, he explains the meaning of the two words [veda and āgama]: "Veda," etc. (verse 58).
We shall now clearly explain that instrument (karaṇa). || 59 ||

Those who know [the truth] have declared that there are five [meditations]: on the worlds, on the luminaries, on the sky, on progeny, and on the self, because of the greatness of the worlds and so forth.
All these are the Great Compilations; thus it is for those who venerate them.

These words "atha" (now/then) are traditionally understood as intended to establish the sequence of the philosophical views; because they are spoken with reference to the worlds and so forth, they constitute the designation "adhiloka" (with respect to the worlds) and so on.
The earth, the Atiratha, the Preceptor, and the mother who is the lower jaw constitute the first form, the Saṃhitā; then follow the subsequent forms beginning with "divāditya" and so forth.
He states which joy should be cultivated: "By day," etc. (62).
The preceding phoneme is known as the prior form (pūrvarūpa), and the following one is known as the subsequent form (uttararūpa). || 63 ||
It should be understood that this refers to the *saṃhitā*; what other *saṃhitā* could there be here?
*Saṃdhi* (junction) is the middle aperture, as well as space (*ākāśa*) and so forth. (64)
He says that both the vision of the subjects and the vision of the self must be practiced: "The union," etc. (63–64).
That by which one joins together, or the joining itself, is here proclaimed as "vāyu" and so forth;
these [elements] are demonstrated by the phrase "itīmāḥ" (thus these) according to what has been stated. || 65 ||
He concludes by stating the meaning of the sentence: "Thus these... (65).

But for him who worships these [deities] with his intellect dedicated to the scriptures, having approached them through the conceit of identity, this fruit is declared: The result for one who, having approached these deities with a mind surrendered to the scriptures, does so through the conceit of identifying with them, is now being stated.
Sitting for a long time for the sake of that goal is called its worship.
He who, being composed, recites these great compendiums of the Vedas as they have been described, will undoubtedly be united with offspring and other blessings ending in heaven.
The mantra "yaśchandasām" is prescribed for one desiring intelligence;
likewise, "āvahantī" is used here for one desiring prosperity, as indicated by the gender [of the deity]. (68)
The meaning is that even a human being is useful for the knowledge of Brahman through traditional succession. || 68 ||

The three Vedas are called *chandas* (metres) because they are characterized by that [metrical form]; and they are called *ṛṣabha* (the bull) and *viśvarūpa* (universal form) because they pervade all speech. (69)
This [Veda] manifested from the immortal Vedas of Prajāpati;
indeed, because the syllable Om is eternal, its production is not described as being direct.
The comparison is explained by way of its preeminence; regarding this, he says: "Of the syllable Om... (verse 70).
Oṃkāra, the lord of all desires, he is Indra, the Supreme Lord;
may he, through wisdom and insight, protect me—that is, may he gladden me. || 71 ||
He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "samendro medhayā" as follows: "The syllable Om," etc. (verse 71).
May I be a sustainer of self-knowledge, which is the sole cause of immortality.
O Lord, may my body always be discerning;
may my mind be gladdened, and my tongue be sweet-spoken. (73)
May I hear the abundant meaning of the Vedas through my two ears;
for you are the treasury of Brahman, like the sheath of a sword for the Supreme Self.
The meaning is that everything is established there by means of inference (karṣāt). || 74 ||
Because they have cast off all desires, they perceive that Supreme Reality in you;
by means of this name as a symbol, they seek to apprehend Him.
You alone attain the state of being the cause; therefore, you are called the "Treasury" (kośa).
Because you are concealed by the worldly intellect and by intelligence,
those whose minds are directed outward do not worship you, the god who bestows immortality.
Attachment to sense objects is mundane wisdom.
O Lord, protect this learning of mine from the causes of passion, hatred, and the like. (77)
"Endowed with that which has been heard, I enter into you alone"—the subsequent action [of the verb] "vahanti" (they carry) signifies the sense of expansion, meaning "they cause one to reach. (78)
O God, may she who performs both [these duties] bring me prosperity for a long time;
and through her knowledge of the meaning of the Vedas, may she grant me food and drink. (79)
This is the remainder [of the verse]. In the absence of that, prosperity is considered to lead to misfortune. || 79 ||
"Endowed with hair and joined with sacrificial animals, and [present] individually at all times"—this utterance "svāhā" is stated for the purpose of making known the conclusion of the mantra. (80)
Regarding the word "kam": he states the intended meaning of the application of the *svāhākāra*—namely, that it occurs at the end of the mantra. || 80 ||
In the same way, even further on, the word "svāhā" occurs because it arises from that;
and by means of divine and human wealth alone, one attains both the otherworldly and the worldly.
Since it is capable of performing action, those two are therefore requested for that purpose.
"May all those who desire to study and hear [the teachings] come here for my sake. || 82 ||
Let the celibate students strive diligently for the sake of excellence;
let them come together by the millions and quickly approach me alone. (83)
He states the meaning of "May they come" (*āmāyantu*) and so forth: "May they come" (*āyantu*). || 82 ||
Some read "dvayam" (a pair); he states its meaning as "for the sake of excellence" (prakṛṣṭyartham). || 83 ||
"May I be known by people as 'famous'—this is the purpose of the former [mantra];
and may I be more excellent than my kinsmen, superior to them in virtue."
In the expression *vasīyaso vasyasaḥ*, the elision of the vowel *i* may occur by Vedic license (*chandasaḥ*).
The suffix *īyasun* may follow either *vasu* or *vasumat*, because it denotes a desired excellence over something of the same class that possesses superior qualities. (85)
Therefore, the meaning is: "May I become even more excellent than Vasumattara. || 85 ||
O Blessed One, I enter into you, who are the treasury of Brahman;
and do you enter into me with your all-pervading self—be gracious to me.
May there be oneness between us; destroy the cause of our difference.
Then, within you who are infinite diversity, I shall wipe away my evil deeds.
The meaning is that by that very [act], there shall be the destruction of my evil karma. || 86 || 87 ||
Just as waters flow swiftly toward the abode of Makara by way of the downward slope, even so may all the celibate students come to me from every direction. 88.
That day in which [all things] decay is called the "day-decayer" (aharjara);
just as months pass within the year, so do they pass within the self that is the day-decayer.
In this context, a "neighbor" (prativeśa) refers to one whose household is nearby;
you are like such a neighbor, for you bring about the removal of all suffering. (90)
Or, because you enter into every living being, you are celebrated as the "Pervader" (Prativeśa);
therefore, shine forth toward me and quickly bring about my destruction. 91.
Now, the meditation upon the self consisting of the vyāhṛtis is being declared for the sake of attaining the fruit of self-sovereignty; therefore, its greatness is here glorified. (92)
The three well-known *vyāhṛtis*—*bhūr*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svar*—are to be known by men; the fourth, however, the sage declared to be *mahaḥ*. (93)
Because he belongs to the Mahācamasa lineage, the secondary derivative (taddhita) suffix may have the sense of "lineage";
thus, the name Māhācamasya directly proclaims his greatness.
He states the meaning of the secondary derivative (taddhita) [in the word "mahācamasa"]: "In the great cup," etc. (94).
This mention of the seers' names may serve as an ancillary element (aṅga) to the meditative worship (upāsanā);
for here, the worship is said to be intermingled with the recollection of the seers (ārṣeya-smṛti).
He states the purpose of mentioning the names of the sages with the words: "Upāsanā" (95).
This fourth utterance, which is "Brahman," should be meditated upon in this way;
it should be known as "the Great" because by means of it one attains the Self. (96)
He states this—namely, that [the self] has the nature of fire—by saying "because of its greatness" (mahattvāt). || 96 ||
Since [he] is pervasive by virtue of being the sun, the moon, Brahmā, and food. || 97 ||
The world, the gods, and so forth are pervaded by that Self; thus, there would be "greatness" (mahaḥ).
And here, the mention of the deities is an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa) for all remaining [entities]. (98)
It establishes its all-pervasiveness with the verse beginning "āditya" (97).
The worlds, the gods, and likewise the Vedas, as well as the vital breaths and the limbs in their entirety—these are to be known as the "mahas" of that very self which consists of the vyāhṛtis. 99.
He states the established meaning regarding the indication of what remains: "The worlds," [verse 99].
Since all the Ādityas are magnified by means of the Supreme Self, and because the word "maha" has been thus spoken, the Self should therefore be known as "Mahaḥ. (100)
He states that "because they are the cause, they possess the nature of the Self" with the words: "they are magnified. || 100 ||
For indeed, all the limbs, beginning with the hands, are magnified by the self;
in the same way, the worlds and so forth are nourished by the self through Āditya. || 1 ||
The meaning is that it is called "Self" (ātman) because it is the cause of growth by way of its nature as the earth and so forth. || 1 ||
This world, the Ṛgveda, and the vital breath—these are the fourfold [forms].
The sacred utterance (vyāhṛti) "bhūḥ" is to be known, and likewise the others in their proper order. (2)
The intermediate space and the wind, as well as the *sāman* and the *apāna*—this second *vyāhṛti*, "bhuvaḥ," is considered to be fourfold. (3)
"Yauḥ," "Ādityaḥ," "Yajuḥ," and "Vyānaḥ"—these four, beginning with "Maheśva," were previously declared; thus there are four types of fourfold [mantras]. || 4 ||
He explains "likewise others" and so forth with the words: "the intermediate space," etc. (3).
He concludes by stating: "There would be four. (4)
The repetition of what has already been stated is intended for the purpose of providing instruction on meditation:
"But that man who meditates upon these aforementioned Vyāhṛtis as the Vedas..."
He knows the entirety of Brahman, characterized by the attributes that are about to be described. || 5 ||
Intending that [the answer] will occur in the subsequent section, he qualifies it as "to be described" (vakṣyamāṇa). || 5 ||
If it is asked why "He knows Brahman" is stated again,
there is no fault, because the intention is to explain the meaning of the subsequent section that is about to be recited.

"He who knows that very one" refers to the reality to be meditated upon in the subsequent section beginning with "He who is within," which will be explained hereafter; the phrase "he knows" is stated again for emphasis.
Therefore, there is syntactical unity between these two sections (anuvākas).
The worlds and the gods and others bestow upon this worshipper offerings and enjoyments according to their power; this is the fruit for the one who worships.
I have explained the three *vyāhṛtis* as the limbs of that Brahman; now, for the sake of establishing its locations and so forth, the supreme composition concerning it is being declared. (10)
That which was indicated indirectly is now shown directly:
behold the Self within the space of the heart by means of the self. 11.
For that piece of flesh shaped like a lotus is called the heart;
in its center is the space which is always the locus of the intellect.
In that [state], he is to be known as this person here consisting of mind (manomaya).
Like Rāhu in the moon, it is perceived directly within the mind itself.
Because one thinks with the mind, it is for that reason "consisting of mind" (manomaya);
or rather, because of the identification with that [mind], it is traditionally remembered as "consisting of that" (tanmaya) based on the indicative mark.
The immortal one is characterized by the nature of non-death; gold is called light (*jyotis*).
This person (*puruṣa*) is to be meditated upon as consisting of that [light]; and the means for attaining it is now described. (15)
A single channel, Suṣumnā, extends upward from the heart; having reached the two palates, O wise one, it passes through their middle, containing the Udāna breath.
A piece of flesh hangs from the neck, facing downward;
this is known as the path of Indra, and by means of it, one should proceed with the exhaling breath (recaka).
The construction of the sentence is: "By means of that [power], one should proceed through the force of the exhalation-prāṇāyāma. || 17 ||
Having gone by that [path], he proceeds; once stilled, he turns back.
Having split the two skull-halves of the head, he enters the fire with the syllable "bhūḥ. || 18 ||
Then, by the second *vyāhṛti*, one becomes firmly established in Vāyu;
by "Suvaḥ," one becomes firmly established in Āditya, the lord of the world.
Having thus remained within the constituent parts, one becomes established in the whole;
then, abiding in the Self as "the Great," one attains self-sovereignty.
He states that one attains Brahman which exists as both the whole and its parts by means of the words beginning with "bhūḥ": || 18 || 19 || 20 ||
There is no other king here whose king he is; rather, he who is himself the king is a self-ruler (svarāṭ), and his state is celebrated here as sovereignty (svārājya).
The sphere of worldly transaction and the sentence are what are referred to here by the two words [loka and vākya]. || 21 ||
One who attends upon [these] attains sovereignty over the mind, speech, the eyes, and also the ears and consciousness; of this there is no doubt.
From the aforementioned meditation, this divine fruit shall arise. 22.
Explaining that "it arises," he concludes with the result: "therefore" (tataḥ). || 22 ||

If there were a relationship of qualifier and qualified, a fault would ensue; but when the defined object attains the status of the definition, not even the slightest fault exists here. (50)
That which resides in multiple substrates possessing distinct natures, which does not grasp its own substrate, and which excludes those of the same class, is here called a qualifier (viśeṣaṇa). (51)
The meaning is that a qualifier (viśeṣaṇa) is precisely that which distinguishes the qualificand (viśeṣya). || 51 ||

That which is connected with both the general and its opposite, endowed with multiple qualities, and possessing both possible and impossible attributes, is declared to be the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). (52)
"Possible" (saṃbhavī) means that the qualificand is distinguished from its own class and so forth. || 52 ||

That which remains as a subordinate element to another qualificand, from which the cognition of its own qualificand arises, and whose relationship is merely conceptualized—that is a definition (lakṣaṇa) serving as a condition for existence (bhāvalakṣaṇa). (53)
Just as one [contradictory factor] is set aside, so too is another that is contradictory;
here it is stated that [the object] is characterized by its own nature alone, in a single form. (54)
That which is intended as the object of definition (lakṣya) is distinguished from everything else; this is the meaning of "the object of definition. || 54 ||
Truth and the other [virtues], because they are for the sake of another, are mutually independent; however, their application is restricted by the object to be qualified. (55)
Whatever form has been once cognized never appears as something else; therefore, it is truly distinct from its effect.
He shows the meaning of the word "truth" (satya) with the words: "once" (sakṛt). || 56 ||
Whatever modification exists here, Brahman is withdrawn from it;
that [Brahman] possesses causality and likewise possesses the attribute of consciousness.
In order to eliminate those two defects, it is declared that "Brahman is knowledge.
But since [the word] is connected with many meanings, for what purpose is it said to be "knowledge"? (58)
He asks, out of a desire to understand the specific meaning, [beginning with] "anekārtha" (58).
Accompanied by the commentary composed by Ānandagiri:
Since it distinguishes Brahman and is conjoined with infinity, it is logical that [the root] *jñā* means "cognition" (*jñapti*), for otherwise defects would be observed. (59)

Therefore, that knowledge which is true and infinite is what is understood here; thus, on the basis of this logical demonstration, it must be taken as a bhāvasādhana (a term denoting the action itself). || 60 ||
In this regard, he shows the reason expressed by the word "ataḥ" (therefore) with the words: "yuktīti" (verse 60).
By the statement "Brahman is knowledge," that [Brahman] attained finitude, for here there is a logical connection with the finitude of worldly knowledge. (51)

Therefore, for the purpose of negating that [limitation], it is designated as "infinite" (ananta). He provides the resolution with the word "infinite" by means of the phrase "ataḥ" (therefore). || 62 ||
Since truthfulness and the like are implied by the prohibition of falsehood and so forth, and since Brahman is not established [as a known entity], that speech which refers to it must be false. (63)
Having restated the desire, he prohibits it: "From untruth," [he says]. || 63 ||
That which does not embrace the ultimate truth is never seen to be false anywhere;
therefore, everything that is false is established solely upon the ultimate truth.
The cognition of the meaning of a word does not arise from each individual phoneme, as is the case with [the perception of] a blue lotus and so forth;
therefore, it is incapable of negating that [phonemic nature], because it consists of the form of the word-meaning and the sentence-meaning. (65)
The meaning is that words such as "truth" (satya) and so forth convey meanings designated as "fullness. || 65 ||
For, having first apprehended an object, one subsequently cognizes the non-existence of its opposite due to their mutual contradiction, just as one recognizes the killer by means of the victim.
First, the connection between the property and the property-bearer is understood from the word;
however, the exclusion [of other referents] is derived from another means of knowledge and is therefore not considered verbal. Thus it is remembered. (67)
The cognition of "blue" does not arise without having apprehended the blue object; likewise, the cognition of the qualified object does not occur without the qualifier. (68)
For us, the experience of the sentence-meaning arises with respect to [objects] such as blue; and it is only when this is so that the expectancy "What is blue? is logically possible. (69)
Since every object must be determined through direct perception, it is by no means possible to establish momentariness in any way whatsoever. (70)
When the jar exists, there is no destruction; nor does destruction have that [jar] as its locus.
If it exists, the substratum is as before, and thus it is not destroyed, being just as it was before. (71)
He says, "If it exists," [meaning] that there would be no distinction between the two subsequent times regarding the bell. || 71 ||
If the destruction of the desired [destruction] were to occur, let there be a hundred lives;
my position is that the jar is indestructible, and that [position] is not at all undermined.
Destruction does not destroy the destroyer, just as motion does not destroy the mover;
for how could that which is established only when something else exists obstruct that very thing? (73)
It establishes the absence of the capacity to cause the cessation of its own substratum with the words: "In which... (verse 73).
Since this statement was previously cited for the purpose of providing a definition, emptiness does not follow as a consequence here, because it relies upon a qualification. (74)

Even though these [attributes] function as qualifiers, they serve as defining characteristics (lakṣaṇa) with respect to the Self; for if that which is to be defined did not exist, it would follow that the attributes such as "truth" and so forth could not have that [Self] as their purpose. (75)
Anticipating the objection, "Could it not be the object of definition? he says: "If the object of definition does not exist," etc. (75).
Therefore, because it expresses a defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa), this statement does not have the meaning of emptiness;
even if it were a qualificand (viśeṣya), it would not be so, because there is no reason for it to abandon its own primary meaning.
If its own referent does not exist, [a term] such as "satya" (real) cannot function as a restrictor for the meaning of the qualificand.
The capacity to restrict a restricted object is only possible when its own referent exists. (77)
He establishes [this] through positive and negative concomitance: "It exists for its own sake. (77)
In this context, the word "Brahman" is meaningful in its own primary sense, as are the other [qualifiers];
therein, "infinite" (ananta) is a qualifier precisely by way of excluding finite things. (78)
The two remaining [words] are qualifiers precisely through the channel of surrendering their own meanings;
the abandonment of meanings that contradict them occurs by implication (sāmarthyāt), not from the word itself.

If Brahman is made known as something distinct from the nature of consciousness, then tell me, by what can the resulting confusion—where [Brahman] becomes accessible through injunction (*niyoga*)—be prevented? (81)
If this suffering self were not inherently powerful by its own nature, then would its constraint or lack of constraint make any difference? (82)
1. First Section: Accompanied by the Commentary (*Ṭīkā*) composed by Ānandagiri.

If one who perceives the inner self (*pratyagātman*), having cast aside all other objects, possesses the realization "I am Brahman" derived from the scriptures, how could there be anything higher than that? (83)

If qualities such as non-materiality and so forth are considered to belong to something other than the self, then what would those qualities avail this [self] if it were not the self? If, however, they were the self, then there would be no negation of the notion of "other. (84)

Because [the teaching] begins with "That which is directly" and concludes with "He who is the Self," and because the meaning of each part is fulfilled by the other, whereas [this would be] impossible if they were distinct. (85)
If you accept that the self alone is the supreme Brahman, then because the self is the agent of knowledge, knowledge would have the agent as its instrumental cause. (86)
If [the self] were the meaning of the verbal root, it would follow that it is dependent and impermanent;
furthermore, according to what is well-known in the treatises on logic, the self would simply be an agent. (87)
Raising their arms high, those who are clever at predicting tomorrow say:
"How could all this that has been declared not be exactly so? (88)
Although it is not distinct from its own nature, it is designated as an "effect" figuratively;
here, effects that depend upon the intellect are conceptualized through a lack of discrimination. (89)
The meaning is that "being an effect" is superimposed upon the gift. || 89 ||
[1ga] Folio; [2] No. Gha; 'Nastutaka; 3 Ga-ca; they are appropriate.
[1] First Section, accompanied by the commentary composed by Ānandagiri:
Knowledge is the very nature of the Self; it is not distinct from it.
The intellect's capacity to produce cognition is figuratively attributed to its witness.
Since the intellect (dhī) produces mental modifications (vṛtti) that are pervaded by the consciousness of the Self,
all of them are embraced by consciousness, like sparks from heated iron.
Seeing the cognitions— which have the intellect as their agent— as being inlaid with consciousness,
the ignorant imagine that knowledge is produced, even though [the Self] is immutable.
Since the manifestation and disappearance of the intellect of human beings have [the Self] as their witness, upon what other [entity] could the status of being a witness-agent be based? (93)
Just as that form was previously unconditioned by the states of the intellect, so too, even when the intellect arises, let it be experienced as indeed changeless. (94)
The meaning is that his reliability [dāstheyam] arises from his being the accomplisher of all actions. || 94 ||
1. *ga*, *ba*: *ṃndayartā*; 2. *ga*, *gha*, *ca*: *to vṛ*; 3. *ca*: *nyaṃ kartṛtve*; *ga*, *gha*: *buddhayā*; 5. *stabhā*; 6. *ka*: *mekañca*; *ca*: *mekace*; 7. *ṅa*, *ca*: *vaivikri*.
Because they manifest as agent and action, [the words] denote the agent and the action.
They perceive the Supreme Brahman, yet they do not describe it directly.
That knowledge of Brahman which is non-different from all things and changeless is not distinct from Brahman itself, because it is fully realized through the direct perception of everything.
By the word "truth" (satya), which denotes the reality that excludes all distinctions of a self,
that [ultimate reality] is indicated in that very same way, but it is not expressed.
The meaning is that it is possible, because the absence of a cause is equal [in both cases]. || 97 ||

Thus, words such as "existent" (satya) and so forth, without abandoning their own primary meanings, indicate another [meaning] by way of the cessation of contradictory objects through the removal of ignorance. (98)
First Section. Accompanied by the commentary composed by Ananyagirī:

Because their referents are distinct from what is to be negated, the [terms] such as "real" (*satya*), which negate objects such as the unreal (*asatya*), have as their meaning that which is different [from those negations].
Therefore, it is established that the Self is not the meaning of a sentence (*avākyārtha*). || 99 ||
This being so, everything is meaningful; otherwise, it would be meaningless. || 100 ||
Immutability is said to be truth; knowledge is declared to have that as its quality.
When awareness is inherently immutable, the knower possesses infinity and unity.

In the Mīmāṃsaka view, the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*) is of two kinds: [the meaning of the individual words] and [the unified meaning]. Regarding the question as to how there can be unity when there is a plurality of meanings, it is stated: "Unity" [is achieved through the relation of the parts]. || 1 ||
However, because there is no distinction among knowers, that [object] is not the most desired;
and since there is no other knower, how can it be said that "he knows"? (2)
Therefore, the statement "he who knows" is untenable; this is the meaning. || 2 ||

The cognition that negates unreal objects and so forth, which arises from ignorance regarding the true object of perception such as reality (satya) and the like, attains only what was already attained by the path [of practice], due to the loss of absolute knowledge (kevalajñāna). || 3 ||
He refutes this, saying "not so," with the words "satyādi" (beginning with truth), etc. || 3 ||
Thus, that which was known he knows; being liberated, he is liberated;
that which had ceased turns back—this I swear to you three times. (4)
Therefore, due to this ignorance which acts as a cataract obscuring one's nearness to agency,
one does not perceive Brahman— characterized by existence and other attributes— even though it resides within oneself.
Therefore,
with the cessation of ignorance, his vision ever-shining,
he drinks [the nectar] and perceives the inner Self as the manifoldness beginning with "this" (atra). || 6 ||
Since it stands as "raṇa," he states the result [of this] with the words "ataḥ" (therefore). || 6 ||
Since the self's cognition of being an agent and an enjoyer arises from its contact with the mere elements, it is therefore deposited within the intellect (buddhi).
That [Brahman], which is entirely free from darkness (tamas) and passion (rajas), is apprehended through that very state [of the mind];
therefore, the Śruti declares: "Brahman is hidden in the intellect by means of the mind alone. (8)
Because they perceive that which is hidden within this [intellect] due to the affliction of desire, ignorance,
and so forth, and because it is the inward-facing intellect that perceives it, therefore the intellect is called "the house" (gṛha).
The supreme ether is that which is within the heart, for it is superior to the external;
as the Veda says, "that which is outside," and that [supreme ether] is the support of the intellect.
Whether with respect to the cave [of the heart] or the supreme firmament, or in consideration of the actual state of things,
nothing other than that which is characterized by truth and so forth is perceived as the inward-facing consciousness.
The ascetic, whose intellect is perfectly turned away from things contrary to truth and the like,
then enters his own inward consciousness and beholds the true Self.
The meaning is that one determines: "Brahman alone is the reality of the witness of the intellect. || 12 ||
Therefore, for the sake of accomplishing the means [to liberation], the Śruti has thus instructed us to cause the intellect to enter within,
into the cave of the heart and the supreme ether.
He states that the scriptural passage beginning with "He who knows this" has a logically consistent meaning: "Therefore... (13).
1. First Section] Accompanied by the commentary composed by Ānandagiri:
In order to remove the notion of duality, that Supreme Brahman—which is to be known within the cave [of the heart] and in the highest ether—remains as the Knower. (14)
The meaning is that since the witness is Brahman alone, there is no possibility of suspecting any difference between the two. || 14 ||
For one who follows the very path of the relationship between the means and the goal,
the Supreme— which is free from both means and goal— enters into his own self.

Fearing that it might be impossible for him to enjoy all desires simultaneously while acting as an agent, [the author] says "by Brahman" and "simultaneously" (saha). He explains the meaning of the word "saha" by saying "simultaneously" (yugapat). || 16 ||
That Brahman would not exist in the inward [Self] if its meaning were one of difference;
nor can that which is turned away from the Self (parāgbhūta) be conceived as possessing such qualities as "Being" and so forth, for it is the Supreme.
Regarding the Brahmin, he states another fault [in the case of such a distinction]: "It is possible," etc. (verse 17).
Nor can it be that [the word *saha*] is unable to express the meaning of "together" because it is a particle (*nipāta*);
therefore, the word *saha*, which denotes the sense of simultaneity, must be what [expresses it]. (18)
Since there exists nothing other than the Self from which ignorance and the like are eliminated through knowledge, therefore the wise one enjoys all desires together with Brahman. (19)
The meaning is that because it is manifested as if divided through the delimitation of its parts, there is a description of it as being manifold. || 19 ||
For the knower, nothing other than the inward-facing [Self] residing within the cave of the heart is found;
for those who know it, Brahman—characterized by truth and so forth—is indeed the innermost Self (pratyagātman).
Since the Self is likewise of that nature, the meaning is that there is not even a scent of difference between the two.
In order to eliminate the possibility that [the Self] is an object of knowledge apart from the All-Seeing One, [it is designated] through grammatical coordination with the All-Seeing Brahman. (21)
By the word "direction" (diś), the state of being reachable by Brahman is understood. || 21 ||

It is observed: "For indeed, by means of one [intellect] functioning sequentially, [the self] pervades those [objects] that function sequentially. [This concludes] the tenth section (*anuvāka*), accompanied by the commentary composed by Ānandagiri. By means of a single [intellect] that functions in succession, it pervades those things that function in succession.
"Having realized all desires, he is one who is desireless," so says the Śruti. || 22 ||
In the beginning, at the end, and likewise in the middle, the various bodies of the intellects are pervaded by the one undifferentiated consciousness,
which is of the nature of non-dual experience.
It establishes the immutability mentioned regarding consciousness with the verse beginning "In the beginning" (23).
Since the knower of Brahman enjoys all causes of worldly activity as well as all desires, therefore there is no activity for the knower of Brahman that is without a cause.
Desires have ignorance as their cause; activities have desire as their root.
Both merit and demerit have those as their root, and from that follows the body, which is the locus of misfortune. (25)

Therefore, upon the cessation of ignorance, there shall be for the wise man a constant cessation; indeed, at that very moment, there is the cessation of all modifications which are the causes of karma without exception. (26)
He establishes this with the passage beginning "Ignorance" (avidyā) and so forth. || 25 || 26 ||
In ancient times, it was declared that this is the aphorism (sūtra) for the entire meaning of the Upaniṣads;
and its meaning has been correctly described in brief by means of the mantra. || 27 ||
Whatever meaning has been indicated here by this opening verse, from that point until the conclusion, this commentary is now being stated. (28)
By the words "by this," he shows the connection [to what has] arisen. || 28 ||
Truth, knowledge, and infinite—beyond the five elements beginning with taste—is that which is described in the scriptures as "unseen" and so forth; "I am Brahman," thus [one becomes] fearless. (29)
But how can that which is real and infinite be correctly understood?
This is now being investigated, given that [understanding] depends upon causes such as place and time. (30)
In reality, infinity is said to be threefold—by way of space, by way of location, and by way of time; therefore, the truth of Brahman is also established. || 31 ||
Space is infinite in terms of its location because it is devoid of spatial limitation;
for an effect, by virtue of its cause, occupies only one location and does not exist elsewhere.
Because it is an effect, it does not exist [eternally] in terms of time; and because there exists another entity apart from it, its infinity does not exist even in terms of substance. (33)
The meaning is that Brahman exists as something distinct from space. || 33 ||
Because time, space, and so forth are its source, because the Self is likewise the self of all,
and because no other entity exists, the supreme Self possesses primary infinity.
Showing the difference between Brahman and space, he says: "Time," etc. (34).
There is no delimitation by means of the imagined, for there is no such thing as an unimagined reality;
time and so forth are imagined, according to the teaching that they are a mere modification of speech. (35)
Therefore, by means of the phrase "therefore" and so forth, the true nature of truth and the rest will be explained with effort under the guise of the creation of Brahman. (36)
The word "vai" (indeed) serves for the purpose of recollection regarding what was stated in the sentence beginning with "tasmāt" (therefore);
whereas "etasmāt" (from this), as stated in the mantra, is characterized by qualities such as truthfulness and the like.
This is understood from both the capacity of the learned and from fear;
for the primary meaning of the term "Self" (ātman) is not found anywhere other than in the inner self (pratīc). (38)
He states that the identity of Brahman and the Self is logical with the words: "Because of the scriptural statement regarding the Self" (sūtra 38).
All this has arisen from me alone, and into me alone it dissolves at the end;
thus it is established that I am the one who knows. (39)
Having taken recourse to the nature of Brahman—which is entirely non-dual, immutable, without effect, and without cause—creation cannot be spoken of. (40)
Everything other than Brahman is intended to be described as an effect;
and because Brahman is not an effect, there is no possibility of a cause for its creation. (41)
1. The primary meaning. 2. Māgha, by Prasapha. 3. Ga, Gha, Li. 4. Ga, Gha, it arises.
[First Section] Accompanied by the commentary composed by Ānandagiri:
If the nature of Brahman is the cause of creation because of its constant proximity, [then creation would be eternal].
The creation is always like that of Brahmā, and it does not arise from a specific location. || 42 ||
He says "not" [in the verse] to show that creation does not occur at all times. || 42 ||
It has not been created because it is unoriginated; it is unoriginated because of the nature of time.
It will not exist because it is non-existent; and it is non-existent because it does not arise from action.
"Will be," "is," and "was"—these [tenses] do not, however, depend upon the actual state of things (vastuvṛtta). || 44 ||
Since the qualifiers "will be," "is," and "was" are as futile as [the word] "camel" applied to the atom (*aṇu*), ignorance alone is the cause here. (45)

There is no cause for that which is non-existent, because that which is existent lacks any further excellence; and because of its immutability, there is neither birth nor destruction, and if there were birth from birth, it would lead to an infinite regress.
Because ignorance arises throughout the three periods of time, karma, the gods, Īśvara, and so forth lack causal agency; for this very reason, they are not the cause [of bondage]. (47)
For these—birth, maintenance, and dissolution—occur for the world at every moment;
indeed, the Śruti declares that the agent produces [the world] through cognition and by means of actions. (48)
From Brahmā, whose self is utterly corrupted by ignorance that has no beginning, middle, or end, space is born, just as the moon [appears] from a visual disorder such as cataracts. (49)
Accompanied by the commentary composed by Ānandagiri:
It is not capable of remaining even for a moment; how then can its effect be permanent?
Arising from the ignorance of the object of experience, it appears permanent to the deluded vision, just as [the snake] in a rope. 50.
Just as one overwhelmed by cataracts perceives his own moonlight as if it were distinct [from himself], so too does he perceive the effect as distinct from himself. (51)
Whatever has arisen in its respective order is traditionally held to possess that many qualities;
for the subsequent elements, being effects, are pervaded by the preceding ones in due sequence. (52)
And because space and the other elements are effects, wind and the rest are not produced from it;
since the birth of wind occurs from that which has the nature of space, therefore that [wind] arises from the Self alone.
One should indeed perceive only the five elements, beginning with space;
nothing other than these elements is admitted to exist, whether in the form of cause or effect. (54)

The meaning is that because [the quality] is contingent upon contact with another substance, its inherent nature is not established. || 55 ||

Just as the earth, though consisting of four qualities, is not [identical] even within those four, so too the entire world has Brahman as its self; thus it is Brahman alone, and not composed of the world.
The meaning is that Brahman’s state of being devoid of distinctions is not contradictory. || 56 ||
That Brahman which was previously declared to be truth, knowledge, and infinite, and which is experienced as non-dual—that has been clearly established through reasoning. (57)

The Lord, the cause of the directions and so forth, who sustains a body composed of the five elements, became Virāj through the conceit "I am everything. (58) *With the commentary composed by Ānandagiri.*

Prior to this [creation] there would be the Sūtra; for when that exists, Virāṭ arises from it, according to another Śruti passage and by way of an indicative mark (liṅga), namely "consciousness" (vijñāna). || 59 ||
He states that the intended meaning of the sūtra is "consciousness" (vijñāna) by saying: "It is consciousness. || 59 ||

For, because [the text] leads [the self] out from the *annamaya* and the others, stating "food, breath," and because of the instruction for meditation (*upāsanā*), the Sūtra is intended here [to mean "instruction"]. (60)
Prior to the production of the effect, the cause—like clay—is real and indivisible;
having produced the effect, it appears as if it has itself become the effect. (61)
The meaning is that [the gross state] is attained by means of the Virāṭ-ātman. || 61 || 1. ga. gha. reads "dikara". 2. ma. pa. ca. reads "tama". 3. ga. reads "bra".
But when there is no [external] effect, that thread, bearing the form of a mass of pure consciousness,
becomes differentiated by its own effects and attains the state of both the collective whole (samaṣṭi) and the individual parts (vyaṣṭi).
Dependent upon rain and other factors, all plants such as rice and the like, which consist of the five elements, arise from the earth in due order. (63)
From them, food and the eater are likewise produced;
from the food that has been consumed, its transformation arises, and from that essence (rasa), blood is born.
From blood flesh is born, and from that comes fat;
from fat the bones are produced, and marrow arises from the bones.
Then the emission of semen occurred, along with the seed and the creator of the physical form.

The person whose intellect is enveloped by the great net of his own ignorance— [Fragmentary notes: 6. *ca*. 'yavya; 7. *tadannam*; 8. *ga*, *gha*, *ṅa*. *ca*. 'rūpapa'; 1. First Section; accompanied by the commentary composed by Ānandagiri.]
His heart was snatched away by the hook of Kāmākhya, which arises from delusion.
Struck by the arrow of the sense-objects with poison called passion—an arrow drawn by the bow of desire through the darkness of ignorance—he was pierced. (67)
Like one possessed by a spirit, rendered powerless by the karma born of his own actions,
he falls swiftly into the company of women, like a moth drawn by the lure of light.
Having drawn that semen from the body according to one's karma and according to what has been heard, it is then discharged by the man into the womb through the channel that carries the seed.
Once it has been emitted into her womb, subject to the power of the causal conditions,
the state of the *kalala* arises, followed by that which takes the form of a *budbuda*.
Subjection to signs means following the previously mentioned knowledge and action. || 70 ||

1'ka. kha. 'struck away'; 2 ga gha 'having uttered "ja"'; 3. gha. "manonā"; "nādyani". From the bubble (*budbuda*) the *peśī* is born; from the *peśī* the solid mass (*ghana*) is born; from the solid mass the limbs are produced, and from the limbs the hair and body-hair arise. (71)
Whatever elements and instruments existed in a previous birth, those very same ones serve for the body here as well; this is established by the force of the scriptural statement, "Just as that. (72)
He states this meaning [of the passage] beginning with "rītyādiśruteḥ" as follows: "In a previous birth... (verse 72).
Even though the Virāj is the self of all, it undergoes limitation due to the delusion that "I am this much," arising from its birth as the Sūtra and its association with desire and action.
He says "of the whole self" to show that there is no limitation [to the pervasion]. || 73 ||
Likewise, because it consists of the *liṅga*, and because it takes the form of both the collective and the individual,
the Unmanifest (*avyakta*)— as the cause of that limitation— possesses the state of deep sleep (*suṣuptatā*).
He says, "Let it be grasped," [expressed as] "tadavaccheda" (by its delimitation). || 74 ||
Even though the Supreme Self is infinite, its status as the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) arises through ignorance;
thus, it is logically consistent that [the Lord] says, "Know Me also as the knower of the field. (75)
"I do not know"—this ignorance alone is considered its cause; it is impermanent, and it is established by its own very manifestation, like an owl at dawn. (76)
He who desires to see ignorance with a vision born of valid means of knowledge will surely behold the darkness situated within the interior of a cave by means of a lamp.
To perceive "this is not-self" here is the manifestation of ignorance;
therefore, that is called ignorance, while knowledge consists solely in the nature of the Self. (78)
Apart from the excessive grasping at a self, no nature of that [ignorance] exists;
thus it is always appropriate to regard ignorance as being like an enemy. (79)

Therefore, the conceptual construction of "existent," "non-existent," and so forth, belonging to those of deluded minds, subsides when investigated; it does not persist within the Self, which is characterized by the realization "I do not know."
With his mind enveloped by that [ignorance], having abandoned his former body,
he enters a womb as a subtle body (liṅgātman), impelled by the winds of karma and other factors.
Food, water, and fire—each of these, when consumed, undergoes a threefold transformation;
thus, each single element attains a threefold modification.

The goddess Bhāratī arises from the portions consisting of feces, flesh, intellect, and ego, as well as from urine, blood, the vital breaths, and the rays; she also arises from the mind, the intellect, the senses, and the power of action.
And the term "vital breath" (prāṇa) is used for the purpose of indicating the various divisions of the vital breaths.

Whichever sense organ is impelled by the mental impressions arising from karma, that [organ] is produced from the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) according to one's karma and according to what has been heard [in scripture]. (85)
For it is from the conceit "I am a hearer" that the faculty of hearing arises;
one should understand the remaining faculties in the same way. (86)
The arising of a body is unarisen, like space, by virtue of its birth from a jar;
therefore, [the categories] such as existence (astitva) and so forth would also not exist, because they [only] occur when there is a birth.
He states that [the suffixes] *asti* and so forth are prohibited for it: "The [roots] *asti* etc. || 87 ||
To the extent that this body of the one dwelling in the womb grows, to that same extent the manifestation of the subtle body (liṅga) also arises. || 88 ||
Then, in the ninth month of the complete formation of the embodied being, the latent impressions (vāsanās) arising from many past births manifest in succession. (89)
The meaning is that manifestation occurs. The word "atha" (then) is intended to indicate an alternative regarding the month. || 89 ||
Having become manifest, yet being ignorant and conditioned by the sufferings of the womb and so forth, he becomes despondent, crying out, "Alas, what misery! and thus grieves for his own self. (90)
He demonstrates its arising within itself: "Manifested," etc. (90).
The sands of parched grain are heated, burning those of impure intent.
Scorched by the digestive fire, the drops of the humor known as bile burn me most intensely as I am submerged in the womb.
The mouths of the worms born of their own excrement pierce them as if with the thorns of the *kūṭa-śālmali* tree,
while they are sawn through the bones of their flanks.
He says that there is also another suffering that is difficult to endure: "audaryeti" (verse 93).
The suffering I experienced in the womb—which was filled with foul odors and inflamed by the digestive fire—is less than that which arises from being cooked in the Kumbhīpāka hell. (94)
The drinking of pus, bile, and phlegm, the eating of what has been vomited, and the state of becoming a worm within filth—all this was experienced by one dwelling in the womb. (95)
He says that one should strive for the rejection of dwelling in a womb: "Putrid" (verse 95).
It does not exceed the great suffering found in all the hells without exception. [96] [First Section] Accompanied by the Commentary composed by Ānandagiri.
Crushed by the machine of bones, surrounded by the fire within the womb,
with all his limbs scorched and enveloped by the fetal membrane.
Desirous of departing and tormented by suffering, he falls headlong below, weeping loudly with his face cast down, like one released from a mechanical device and lying flat on his back.
He shows the manner of his birth with the words: "While departing" (98).
At that time, the child is ignorant of anything and remains like a mere lump of flesh;
he is protected from dogs, cats, and other fanged predators by those who carry staffs in their hands.
He regards the rākṣasa as his father and the ḍākinī as his mother;
he eats pus as if it were milk—fie upon this most sinful childhood! 200.
He explains the state of infancy for one who has been born: "knowing nothing" (akiñcijjña). || 99 || 200 ||
Then, having attained youth, he became arrogant and overwhelmed by the fever of passion;
he suddenly began to sing loudly and likewise began to leap about. (1)
Blinded by lust, anger, and pride, he climbs a tree with speed and agitates even those who are peaceful; being thus deluded, he does not perceive anything at all.
He elaborates upon the stage of youth following childhood: "Arrogant," etc. (1–2).
Then, having reached old age—a state of great humiliation—he becomes afflicted with suffering;
his chest is constricted by phlegm, and the food he has eaten does not digest.
One who eats pungent, bitter, and astringent foods develops a sour vision; his waist and neck become bent by wind, and he becomes weak with cracked feet. (4)
1. Most excellent; "the most wretched. 2. Ka, Ā, Gha: "on all sides.
Surrounded by ten thousand maces, despised by his own kinsmen, devoid of purity, his limbs smeared with filth, and embraced by the Earth while he lay prostrate. || 5 ||
The downward-moving wind of coughing is the drum; white beard, hair, and garments are the flute; the sound arising from the breath is the lute; and the sound of the stomach is the singer. (6)
Bearing skin like that of one with wrinkles and grey hair, wearing a fine bodice, she stumbles again and again, supported by a staff as her third leg. (7)
Richly adorned with golden ornaments refined by fire, covered with fine skin and cloth,
she made the sound of moving anklets as her ankles and knees rubbed against one another.
Having devoured the wisdom, intelligence, fortitude, valor, and likewise the strength of the young,
old age dances with joy as if its purpose were accomplished.
Even beyond that, no illustration for the suffering of death can be found;
for living beings tremble before it, even when they have already reached the height of agony.
A living being is carried away by death, even while embraced by kinsmen,
just as a serpent dwelling within the waters of the ocean is seized by Garuḍa.

"O beloved! O wealth! O son!"—crying out most piteously, a man is swallowed by death like a frog by a serpent. (12) [Included as requested: ānandagirikṛtaṭīkāsaṃvalitam |] Accompanied by the commentary composed by Ānandagiri.
Let those who desire liberation remember that suffering which belongs to one being slaughtered, as the vital points are being cut and the joints are being severed. (13)
When you are seen being shaken about,
carried away by delusion, and bound by the noose of death, you will find no protector.
Obstructed by darkness as if entering a great abyss,
you will then behold your kinsmen with dejected eyes and a bowed chest.
Then you will see yourself being dragged from all sides by Time with its iron noose, and by kinsmen with the noose of affection. (16)
For one oppressed by hiccups, parched by labored breathing, and dragged away by the noose, there is truly no refuge whatsoever. (17)
Mounted upon the machine of saṃsāra and presided over by the messengers of Yama, he is joined with the noose of Time and afflicted by the suffering of "Where shall I go? (18).
In this world which is like an illusion, who could have a fixed commitment?
Indeed, the world of living beings is like a tree providing rest. 19.
Death is the seed of birth, and likewise birth is the seed of death;
like a waterwheel, man wanders incessantly and without rest. (21)
He summarizes the course of worldly existence with the word "death" (mṛti). || 21 ||
By the deities, oblations known as faith, the moon, rain, food, and semen were offered into the fire of heaven, the clouds, the earth, mortals, women, and the senses. 22.
In this manner, upon the fifth oblation, one is born as a male;
it is said that for him, there follows the gradual cessation of the cycle of existence, which is a great calamity. (23)
All such transformations as these have their locus in the subtle body (liṅgadeha).
Although he does not possess them, through delusion he imagines himself to possess them. (24)
For one acts toward knowledge and action out of the conceit "I am the knower";
then, out of delusion, thinking "I am the thinker," one performs mental activities. (25)
Through the conceit of being the vital breath (prāṇa), it engages in the activity of action;
and through the conceit of being the eye, it is intent upon the perception of forms.

The mind's state of being devoid of the apprehension of solitude is its lack of awakening. || 27 ||
Through the ignorance of identifying with cattle, wealth, and so forth— thinking "I am the possessor of these"—
one thinks, "I am a student, I am a householder, likewise I am an ascetic, and I am a sage."
He considers the consecration of the body, the liṅga, and the self to be the cause of attachment. || 28 ||
The body is said to be the effect of the elements which are distinct from the self; yet, through the delusion of "I" and "mine," one encounters misfortune. || 29 ||

Although all beings are equally subject to the necessity of food and equal in their nature as Brahman, it is only the male person who is understood here, because he alone possesses the qualification for ritual action and knowledge.
He states the intended meaning of the mention of "the person" [in the sūtra] with the words: "And of all... (30).

Just as one might point out the moon by merely indicating the tip of a tree branch.
Just as a sword is shown by pointing to its sheath, Brahman is shown within the inner self (pratīci). || 32 ||
Anticipating the objection that "the ritual placement (nyāsa) is useless," he says: "Like the branch of a tree" (verse 32).
In this beginningless saṃsāra, the mind is colored by latent impressions (vāsanā); it can be made to turn back through skillful means (upāya), and therefore that is called [the means]. (33)

The inner Self alone is non-dual and untouched by duality; though it appears as both the inward and the outward, it is falsely divided by the distinction between "you" (the object) and "I" (the subject) through ignorance.
The meaning is that since the self is false by virtue of being produced by ignorance (avidyā), there is no loss of non-duality (advaita). || 34 ||
Just as the Annamaya and the others [are designated] in our division, so too are the Pratyagātmanas and the Yūṣmad-anna and others traditionally taught in your division. (35)
Then, having dissolved the internal elements each into their respective inner selves,
one should indeed meditate upon the [subtle essences] beginning with food, as they proceed in successive stages.

Having thus consumed the state of being the effect and remaining in the state of being the cause, one embraces Brahman through the self; and having consumed even that [state of causality] by means of the [great] statement, one remains as Brahman alone.

Food is to be known as Virāj; it increases from the vital breath (prāṇa). Therefore, the Self of the Vedas, consisting of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma, is internal and composed of mind (manomaya). || 38 ||
By the word "manomaya," the mind (manas) is understood. || 38 ||
Vijñāna is the intellect whose object is the meaning of the Vedas, characterized by certainty;
bliss, produced from knowledge and action, is characterized as the fruit. || 39 ||

These three foods alone belong entirely to Prajāpati:
breath, mind, and speech; they have attained the nature of food as the Virāj.
The meaning of the word "ca" (and) is that this very [point] has been stated as the reason for that. || 40 ||

Thus, among the four [sheaths], the innermost self alone is called "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya), because its nature is a mass of pure consciousness; yet there may be a distinction between it and the others based on their functions.
The construction of the head and other parts, however, is for the purpose of the rite of meditation;
therefore, one should explain these mental layers (citīs) in this manner. 42.
He states that this is also well-known among the elders by saying: "Therefore... (42).
The head is the crown, the two arms are the wings, and the self is the body in the middle;
the remainder is to be known as the tail—one should contemplate consciousness in this manner. (43)
Seated thus upon these layers, one who knows this enters deeper and deeper by abandoning each preceding one in due order. (44)
The purport of [the passage] beginning with "tyādeḥ" is as follows: Since the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) cannot be doubted, that which has been stated may indeed be possible.
However, regarding what is known through indicative marks (*liṅga*) or direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), doubt might arise from human intellect. (Verse 45)

Or rather, the Śruti, having restated that which is already established by its very nature, enjoins meditation upon the Self as the "Great" (bhūman), just as it does for Name and the other categories. 46.

Or, having been obtained from another Vedic text for the sake of results inferior to liberation, that [meditation] is restated here so that knowledge may be taught for the attainment of the supreme good. (47)

Then, desiring to lead [the seeker] to the further shore of the great ocean of the sheaths of misfortune by means of the boat of the knowledge of Brahman, [the Teacher] spoke the words "That indeed is this. (48) [This is] accompanied by the commentary composed by Ānandagiri.

Having touched the fundamental self (mūlātman) through sound, he then enters into the state of being the sheath (kośātmatā) for the sake of remembering that; thus he is designated as "this one" (eṣa).
The meaning is that this [Self] is taught by means of words such as "the Knower" (kṣatṛ). || 49 ||

Through ignorance, though it is unworthy of it, [the Self] has entered into the state of the five sheaths, like a rope appearing as a snake; therefore, [the author] indeed feels compassion for it. (50)
Anticipating the objection that [the self] ought to attain the nature of the sheath, he says: "by ignorance" (avidyayā). || 50 ||
In this context, that [transformation] is denied for the Supreme Self;
however, through both reasoning and scripture, the body is understood to be the effect of food. (51)
The meaning is that because the self also possesses that as its limiting adjunct (upādhi), its designation as such is established. || 51 ||
"Let this very head of his not be characterized by superimposition (adhyāsa), but rather as being like the sheath of vital breath (prāṇakośa)"; it is from this [statement] that it is determined. (52)

The meaning is that this conceptual construction is for the sake of the true goal and for the sake of making the discernment of the meanings of words easy. || 55 ||
Furthermore, a verse that restates what has been said above is also recited here, out of a desire for the welfare [of others], on the day of understanding the meaning spoken by the Brāhmaṇa. (56)
